newsitem.title: LUXEMBOURG: EU seeks to scale back fish quota cuts, UK defiant.
newsitem.headline: EU seeks to scale back fish quota cuts, UK defiant.

text.p: European Union fisheries ministers on Monday sought to tone down plans to slash fish catches by up to 30 percent while Britain said it would not implement further cuts until so-called "quota hoppers" had been dealt with.

EU officials said that France and Germany proposed a maximum reduction of 15 percent between 1997-99, saying that anything more would be impossible. The EU's executive Commission originally proposed a 40 percent cutback over six years.

British Fisheries Minister Tony Baldry said a solution must first be found for quota hoppers and until then Britain would block progress on an inter-governmental conference (IGC) reviewing the European Union Treaty.
"We are not going to allow the IGC to conclude until the whole issue of quota hopping is resolved," Baldry told reporters, "We will not waiver."
The IGC, which is due to end in June, is discussing changes in the way the EU operates in preparation for the admission to the Union of up to 10 east European countries.

Britain strongly objects to the practice of quota hopping under which fishing vessels from other member states, notably Spain and the Netherlands, register under the British flag and are able to take British fish catch quotas.

"This is a crazy situation whereby over a quarter of the U.K. fishing fleet tonnage is now effectively foreign owned, skippered and controlled," Baldry said. "Everyone in the U.K. wants to see U.K. fish for U.K. fishermen."
Baldry, whose Conservative Party is battling for re-election at national polls on May 1, stressed, "We are determined to stand up in Europe for vital U.K. interests."
EU Fisheries Commissioner Emma Bonino said that the problem of quota hoppers had nothing to do with her proposal to reduce overcapacity and ensure a future for Europe's fishing industry.
"It's no secret that there are elections in Britain," she noted.
Spanish Fisheries Minister Loyola de Palacio hinted that British policy was contradictory.
"I respect the Luxembourg Court's judgement on a free market in the EU. What is surprising is the point of view of a country which professes liberal trade policies," she told reporters.
In July 1991 the European Court of Justice came out against British moves to crack down on quata hoppers, saying that under EU rules it could not discriminate against Spanish fishermen.
Bonino insisted that any compromise agreement on fishing curbs must involve "serious" cuts and not just be "cosmetic."
Spokesman Filippo di Robilant said that Bonino was disappointed that deep differences still remained over the size, shape and duration of the cuts.
"Commissioner Bonino is hopeful rather than optimistic," he said.
A Dutch spokesman said that private bilateral talks would continue late into the night with member states most involved and that a fresh compromise plan would probably be presented on Tuesday.
